entries.title: The velouté family
entries.summary: The daughters of velouté: suprême and allemande on the chicken and veal side, vin blanc, Bercy and normande on the fish side, and a run of small sauces each made by one addition. Learn the stock, then the finish.
entries.guest: A velouté sauce is a pale, silky sauce made from a light stock of chicken, veal or fish, finished with cream, egg yolk, white wine or butter.

paras: Velouté is seldom served as it is. It is a working base, and the sauces a guest meets are its daughters, each finished at the last moment with one or two things that give it a name: cream makes it rich, egg yolks thick and golden, white wine and fish stock taste of the sea, tomato turns it pink. Know the stock and the finish, and any name can be read.

The family splits along the stock: chicken and veal veloutés give suprême and allemande and most of the meat side; fish velouté, made with fumet, a concentrated fish stock, gives the white wine sauces of poached fish.

Suprême is chicken velouté reduced with cream and a little mushroom cooking liquor, then finished with butter. For 1 litre (about 1 quart) of velouté, add about 250 ml (1 cup) of cream in stages as it reduces, and stop when it is nappe, coating the back of a spoon. Off the heat, swirl in 50 g (about 2 oz) of cold butter: ivory, creamy and clean.

Allemande, which Escoffier also called sauce parisienne, is veal velouté bound with egg yolks and lemon. Whisk 4 or 5 yolks with a little cold stock and mushroom liquor, then temper them: whisk in a ladle of hot velouté so they warm gradually, and pour it all back into the pan. This egg finish is a liaison. Bring it back to a simmer, stirring, and reduce it until it coats the spoon: the flour protects the yolks, though a long, hard boil can still grain them. Finish with lemon, nutmeg and butter, and strain.

From allemande comes poulette, with more mushroom liquor, lemon and chopped parsley, the classic sauce for mussels. From suprême comes ivoire, tinted the colour of old ivory with pale chicken glaze, glace de volaille, and from ivoire comes Albuféra, finished with a red pepper butter. Aurore is velouté with tomato cooked down to a paste, pink as the dawn it is named for. Hongroise is onion and paprika softened in butter, white wine reduced over them, then velouté, simmered and strained.

On the fish side, vin blanc is fish velouté with fumet and yolks, finished with butter. Bercy starts with shallot sweated in butter, white wine and fumet reduced over it, then fish velouté, butter and parsley. Normande, the richest, adds mushroom and oyster liquor, yolks and cream. Warm ravigote is velouté with a white wine and vinegar reduction, finished with shallot butter and chopped chervil, tarragon and chives, three of the fines herbes.

Read them by eye and tongue. Suprême is ivory and creamy; allemande is deeper yellow, with a lemon edge; poulette is the same, flecked green. Aurore is coral, hongroise soft salmon and warm with paprika. The fish sauces are pale, glossy and taste of the sea; Bercy shows specks of shallot, ravigote flecks of herb.

Every fault of the velouté passes to its daughters, so mend the base first. The flour in a velouté protects a yolk liaison, so allemande and normande can be reduced with their yolks in, but a long, hard boil still grains them into specks: strain at once and whisk in a little cold cream. A liaison of yolk and cream with no flour behind it, as on a velouté soup, curdles above about 85°C (185°F), so it goes in off the boil. A cream sauce reduced too far turns heavy and oily; loosen it with hot stock. Wine added late tastes raw, so reduce it first.

Sole Véronique, poached sole in a white wine sauce with peeled muscat grapes, glazed under the grill, is the classical ancestor of the Redfish Véronique. Tradition credits it to Escoffier at the Carlton Hotel in London and names it for André Messager's comic opera Véronique; tellings differ on the year and the chef, so tell it as a story.

The Redfish Véronique at Brennan's keeps the idea, fish with grapes, with three changes: redfish for sole, a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the creamy sauce, and grapes pickled in hibiscus instead of fresh. Its sauce has left the velouté family for the butter sauces.

Lead with the stock and the finish: a silky sauce of chicken stock and cream, a white wine sauce of fish stock, a velouté brightened with lemon and parsley. Any question about what goes into a sauce goes to the kitchen.

ratios.label: Suprême, for 1 litre (about 1 quart) of chicken velouté
ratios.value: About 250 ml (1 cup) of cream, reduced to nappe, then 50 g (about 2 oz) of cold butter

ratios.label: Allemande liaison, for 1 litre (about 1 quart) of veal velouté
ratios.value: 4 or 5 egg yolks, loosened with a little cold stock and mushroom liquor

ratios.label: Aurore
ratios.value: About 4 parts velouté to 1 part tomato purée cooked down until thick

ratios.label: The pattern
ratios.value: A velouté of the right stock, then one or two finishes: cream, yolks, wine, butter or a flavour

temps.label: A yolk and cream liaison with no flour, kept at or below

faults.cause: A yolk sauce boiled long and hard after the liaison, or a liaison with no flour taken past about 85°C (185°F).
faults.fix: Strain at once and whisk in a little cold cream; if it has truly curdled, bind it again with fresh tempered yolks.

faults.cause: Reduced too far after the cream went in.
faults.fix: Loosen it with hot stock a spoonful at a time until it coats the spoon again.

faults.cause: The wine went in late and never reduced.
faults.fix: Reduce the wine before the velouté goes in; if it is already in, simmer a few minutes longer and taste.

faults.cause: The velouté itself was poorly skimmed, made with a roux taken too far, or made from weak stock.
faults.fix: Mend the base first: skim off centre and strain, or make the velouté again from good stock.

cards.front: What is the velouté family?
cards.back: The sauces made by finishing a velouté of chicken, veal or fish with cream, yolks, wine, butter or a flavour; velouté itself is rarely served plain.

cards.front: What is sauce suprême?
cards.back: Chicken velouté reduced with cream and a little mushroom liquor until it coats a spoon, then finished with butter: ivory and creamy.

cards.front: What turns veal velouté into allemande?
cards.back: A liaison of egg yolks with mushroom liquor, then lemon juice and nutmeg. Escoffier also called it sauce parisienne.

cards.front: Once the yolks are in, how is an allemande cooked?
cards.back: Brought back to a simmer and reduced, stirring, until it coats the spoon; the flour protects the yolks, though a long, hard boil can still grain them.

cards.front: What is sauce poulette?
cards.back: Allemande with extra mushroom liquor, lemon juice and chopped parsley, the classic sauce for mussels.

cards.front: How is sauce aurore made, and why the name?
cards.back: Velouté with tomato purée cooked down until thick, which tints it pink; aurore means dawn.

cards.front: How are ivoire and Albuféra built?
cards.back: Ivoire is suprême with a little pale chicken glaze, glace de volaille; Albuféra is ivoire finished with a red pepper butter.

cards.front: What gives sauce hongroise its colour and taste?
cards.back: Onion and paprika softened in butter, with white wine reduced over them before the velouté goes in: a soft salmon colour and a warm paprika taste.

cards.front: Name three fish velouté sauces and what marks each.
cards.back: Vin blanc: fumet, yolks and butter. Bercy: shallot, white wine and fumet. Normande: mushroom and oyster liquor, yolks and cream.

cards.front: What is a warm ravigote?
cards.back: Velouté with a white wine and vinegar reduction, finished with shallot butter and chervil, tarragon and chives. The New Orleans ravigote is a different, cold sauce.

cards.front: What is Sole Véronique, and how does the Redfish Véronique differ?
cards.back: Poached sole in a white wine sauce with peeled muscat grapes. Brennan's uses redfish, hibiscus-pickled grapes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc.

cards.front: How do you tell suprême from allemande by eye and taste?
cards.back: Suprême is ivory and creamy; allemande is a deeper yellow from the yolks and carries a lemon edge.

questions.q: Which sauce is chicken velouté reduced with cream and mushroom liquor, then finished with butter?
questions.why: Suprême is the cream daughter of chicken velouté; aurore adds tomato, Bercy is a fish sauce with shallot, and hongroise adds onion and paprika.

questions.q: What binds veal velouté into sauce allemande?
distractors: Whipped cream folded in at the end
Cold butter mounted off the heat
questions.why: Allemande is velouté thickened by a liaison of yolks, which makes it golden and rich and the base of poulette.

questions.q: Once the yolk liaison is in an allemande, how is the sauce cooked?
questions.answer: Reduced at a simmer, stirring, until it coats
distractors: Off the heat, kept below 60°C (140°F) like hollandaise
At a hard rolling boil for ten minutes
Barely warm, so the yolks never thicken
questions.why: The flour in the velouté protects the yolks, so classical allemande is reduced with them in until it coats the spoon; only a long, hard boil grains it.

questions.q: Which sauce is velouté tinted pink with thick tomato purée?
questions.why: Aurore means dawn, for the colour the tomato gives; ivoire takes pale glaze, poulette parsley and lemon, normande oyster liquor and cream.

questions.q: Poulette is built on which sauce of the velouté family?
questions.why: Poulette is allemande with more mushroom liquor, lemon juice and chopped parsley, so it inherits the yolk liaison.

questions.q: Which fish sauce starts with shallot sweated in butter, then white wine and fumet reduced over it?
questions.why: Bercy is built on shallot and a white wine and fumet reduction; the other three belong to the chicken and veal side of the family.

questions.q: Albuféra is ivoire finished with what?
questions.why: Ivoire is suprême with pale chicken glaze, and Albuféra goes one step further with a butter flavoured with sweet red pepper.

questions.q: What goes in at the end of a warm ravigote?
distractors: Tomato purée and a pinch of paprika
questions.why: Warm ravigote is velouté sharpened with a white wine and vinegar reduction, then finished with shallot butter and chopped chervil, tarragon and chives, three of the fines herbes.

questions.q: What did Brennan's change in turning the classical Sole Véronique into the Redfish Véronique?
questions.answer: Redfish, hibiscus grapes, preserved lemon beurre blanc
distractors: Redfish, fresh muscat grapes, a cream sauce
Sole, hibiscus grapes, a brown butter sauce
Pompano, golden raisins, preserved lemon beurre blanc
questions.why: The house keeps the idea of fish with grapes but swaps the sole, pickles the grapes in hibiscus and uses a preserved lemon beurre blanc.

entries.title: The brown family
entries.say: As it reads: the brown family.
entries.summary: The small sauces built on demi-glace: Robert, charcutière, chasseur, diable, piquante, lyonnaise, poivrade, bigarade and the game sauces. Each follows one pattern: an aromatic, an acid reduction, the brown base and a finish.
entries.guest: A brown sauce is a rich, glossy sauce made from roasted bones and wine, given its character by mustard, mushrooms and tarragon, pepper or bitter orange.

paras: The brown family is the set of small sauces made from demi-glace, brown stock and espagnole reduced together until glossy. Demi-glace on its own is deep and meaty but heavy; each daughter cuts it with something sharp and gives it a character. Most classical brown sauces on a menu, in a bistro or a steakhouse, are one of these or a cousin.

Every member follows the same pattern, and a cook who knows it can make any of them from memory: an aromatic cooked in butter, an acid reduced over it, the brown base simmered in, and a finish added at the end. Change one of the four and the sauce changes its name.

Take Robert as the model. Cook a finely chopped onion gently in butter until soft and barely coloured. Add white wine, often with a splash of vinegar, and reduce it by about two-thirds, until the pan is almost syrupy: reduction concentrates the acid and drives off the raw taste of the wine. Add the demi-glace and simmer for about 10 minutes, skimming. Off the heat, whisk in Dijon mustard, and do not let the sauce boil again, or the mustard turns harsh and grainy.

The proportions hold across the family: for 500 ml (about 2 cups) of demi-glace, about 150 ml (2/3 cup) of wine, or wine and vinegar, reduced by two-thirds over two shallots or a small onion. Season at the end, because demi-glace is already concentrated and reduces further as it simmers.

Robert, onion, white wine, demi-glace and mustard, is the old partner of grilled pork. Charcutière, the pork butcher's sauce, is Robert with gherkins (cornichons) cut into fine strips. Chasseur, the hunter's sauce, is sliced mushrooms and shallot sautéed in butter, white wine reduced, tomato and demi-glace, finished with chopped tarragon and parsley: the sauce of chicken chasseur. Diable, the devil's sauce, is white wine and shallot reduced, demi-glace and a good pinch of cayenne, for grilled chicken. The French piquante is vinegar, white wine and shallot reduced, demi-glace, then chopped gherkins and herbs; the Cajun sauce piquante is another dish.

Lyonnaise is onions cooked golden in butter, white wine and vinegar reduced over them, then demi-glace: where Robert keeps the onion pale and adds mustard, lyonnaise browns it and stops. Poivrade, the pepper sauce, starts with a mirepoix browned with game trimmings, then vinegar and the marinade reduced and demi-glace simmered in, with crushed peppercorns added only for the last few minutes. Bigarade, named for the bitter orange, is duck juices or demi-glace with the juice and fine strips of zest of bitter oranges, balanced by a gastrique, sugar cooked to caramel and dissolved with vinegar. It is the sauce of canard à l'orange.

Grand veneur, the master of the hunt's sauce, is the family at its richest: a game poivrade finished with redcurrant jelly and cream, served with venison. The game sauces keep the family's shape with deeper stock, the marinade in the reduction and a sweet or rich finish against the strong meat.

Bitterness comes from a scorched reduction, burnt shallot or pepper simmered too long; strain and soften it with a knob of butter, or start the reduction again. A gluey sauce comes from demi-glace reduced too far or heavy with roux; loosen it with brown stock. Too sharp means the acid was not reduced enough; simmer longer or balance with more demi-glace. Mustard boiled after it goes in turns grainy and harsh.

A guest rarely meets these names, so describe the build: a rich brown sauce of roasted stock and white wine, with mustard, or with mushrooms and tarragon, or with bitter orange for the duck. At Brennan's the brown side shows in the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, a cousin with its own entry. Questions about what a sauce is made with go to the kitchen.

ratios.label: Acid
ratios.value: About 150 ml (2/3 cup) of white wine, or wine and vinegar, reduced by two-thirds

ratios.label: Aromatic
ratios.value: 2 shallots or 1 small onion, finely chopped and cooked in butter

ratios.label: Simmer once the base is in
ratios.value: About 10 minutes, skimming, then the finish off the heat

faults.cause: A scorched reduction, burnt shallot, or peppercorns simmered too long.
faults.fix: Strain and soften with a knob of butter; if it is still bitter, start the reduction again with fresh demi-glace.

faults.cause: Demi-glace reduced too far, or a base heavy with roux.
faults.fix: Loosen with hot brown stock until it coats a spoon and flows.

faults.cause: The wine or vinegar was not reduced enough before the base went in.
faults.fix: Simmer a little longer, or balance with more demi-glace and taste again.

faults.cause: The sauce boiled after the mustard went in.
faults.fix: Whisk the mustard in off the heat at the very end, and hold the sauce hot without boiling.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907), Project Gutenberg eBook 71395

cards.front: What four-part pattern do the brown daughters share?
cards.back: An aromatic cooked in butter, an acid reduced over it, the demi-glace simmered in, and a finish at the end.

cards.front: How is sauce Robert built?
cards.back: Onion softened in butter, white wine (often with vinegar) reduced, demi-glace simmered in, and Dijon mustard whisked in off the heat.

cards.front: What turns Robert into charcutière?
cards.back: Gherkins, cornichons, cut into fine strips and added at the end: the pork butcher's sauce.

cards.front: What goes into sauce chasseur?
cards.back: Sliced mushrooms and shallot sautéed in butter, white wine reduced, tomato and demi-glace, finished with tarragon and parsley.

cards.front: What defines sauce diable?
cards.back: A white wine and shallot reduction with demi-glace and a good pinch of cayenne: the devil's heat, for grilled chicken.

cards.front: How does the French sauce piquante differ from the Cajun one?
cards.back: The French piquante is demi-glace with vinegar, shallot, gherkins and herbs; the Cajun sauce piquante is a spicy tomato stew, a separate dish.

cards.front: How does lyonnaise differ from sauce Robert?
cards.back: Lyonnaise cooks the onions golden and adds no mustard; Robert keeps them pale and finishes with mustard.

cards.front: When do the crushed peppercorns go into a poivrade, and why?
cards.back: Only for the last few minutes of simmering, so they give heat and aroma without turning the sauce bitter.

cards.front: What is sauce bigarade?
cards.back: Duck juices or demi-glace with bitter orange juice and zest, balanced by a gastrique: the sauce of canard à l'orange.

cards.front: What is a gastrique?
cards.back: Sugar cooked to caramel and dissolved with vinegar, used to balance sweet and sour in sauces such as bigarade.

cards.front: What is sauce grand veneur?
cards.back: The family at its richest: a game poivrade finished with redcurrant jelly and cream, served with venison.

cards.front: Why must sauce Robert not boil after the mustard goes in?
cards.back: Boiling turns mustard harsh and grainy, so it is whisked in off the heat at the very end.

questions.q: Which order describes how a brown daughter sauce is built?
distractors: Demi-glace first, then acid, aromatic, finish
questions.why: The aromatic cooks first, the acid reduces over it, the brown base simmers in, and the finish goes in last, off the heat.

questions.q: Which finish, whisked in off the heat, marks sauce Robert?
questions.why: Robert is onion, white wine and demi-glace finished with mustard off the heat; jelly marks grand veneur, orange bigarade and tarragon chasseur.

questions.q: Charcutière is sauce Robert with what added?
questions.why: Gherkins, cornichons, give the pork butcher's sauce its sharp crunch; marrow belongs to bordelaise and mushrooms to chasseur.

questions.q: Which brown sauce is built on sautéed mushrooms and shallot, white wine, tomato and tarragon?
questions.why: Chasseur, the hunter's sauce, carries mushrooms, tomato and tarragon; diable is cayenne, lyonnaise golden onion and poivrade crushed pepper.

questions.q: Why do the crushed peppercorns go into a poivrade only near the end?
distractors: They thicken the sauce too fast
questions.why: Added for the last few minutes, the pepper gives heat and aroma; simmered for long, it leaches bitterness into the sauce.

questions.q: Which sauce is served with canard à l'orange?
questions.why: Bigarade is named for the bitter orange: duck juices or demi-glace with its juice and zest, balanced by a gastrique.

questions.q: What is the gastrique that balances a bigarade?
distractors: Flour cooked in butter to brown
Egg yolk whisked with lemon juice
questions.why: The caramel brings sweetness and the vinegar sharpness, so the gastrique balances the bitter orange and the rich duck.

questions.q: What separates lyonnaise from sauce Robert?
distractors: Bitter orange and a caramel gastrique
questions.why: Both start with onion, but lyonnaise browns it and stops, while Robert keeps it pale and finishes with mustard.

questions.q: On a classical French menu, what is sauce piquante?
questions.answer: A brown sauce with vinegar and gherkins
distractors: A spicy Cajun tomato and pepper stew
A cold mayonnaise with capers and herbs
questions.why: The French piquante is a brown sauce of the demi-glace family; the Cajun sauce piquante is a separate dish taught in its own entry.

entries.title: Madère, Périgueux and the wine-finished sauces
entries.summary: Brown sauces finished with fortified wine: madère, Périgueux and périgourdine with truffle, financière, and the Madeira, port and sherry that finish sauces and soups. The rule: add the wine late and never boil it hard.
entries.guest: Madeira, port and sherry are fortified wines, strengthened with grape spirit. A spoonful added at the end gives a sauce or a soup a nutty, caramel depth.

paras: A fortified wine is wine strengthened with grape spirit: Madeira from the Portuguese island, port from the Douro valley in northern Portugal, sherry from around Jerez in southern Spain. Their sweetness, nuttiness and perfume suit the end of a sauce. Stirred into demi-glace at the last moment, a measure of Madeira turns a meaty base into sauce madère, and the richest brown sauces, Périgueux and its cousins, are built on that.

One rule runs from Escoffier's sauces to a bowl of New Orleans turtle soup: a fortified wine used as a finish goes in late and is never boiled hard, because the perfume a cook pays for is the first thing heat drives off.

For madère, reduce 1 litre (about 1 quart) of demi-glace until it is noticeably thicker than the finished sauce should be, because the wine will thin it. Take the pan off the heat and add about 150 ml (2/3 cup) of Madeira, roughly seven parts base to one of wine. Strain, and hold it hot without letting it boil again. The sauce should be glossy, coat a spoon and smell of the wine, not merely taste of it.

Port and sherry follow the same rule: a ruby or tawny port, a dry amontillado or oloroso sherry, added at the end, tasted and corrected. Where a recipe wants a deeper, sweeter note, a cook may instead reduce the wine first with shallot and then add the base. That is a different sauce, a reduction, and it trades perfume for concentration.

Périgueux, named for the capital of Périgord, the black truffle country of south-west France, is madère with truffle essence, the liquor of cooked truffles, and chopped black truffle. Périgourdine is the same sauce with the truffle in slices or shaped into small balls, and some texts add foie gras. Financière, the financier's sauce, is a Madeira sauce made richer with truffle; it dressed an old garnish of chicken quenelles, mushrooms and truffle served in a vol-au-vent, a puff pastry case. All three are madère first, and the truffle is the finish.

A glaze is the exception to the rule. Reduce the wine with butter or stock until it is syrupy and clings to a vegetable or a piece of meat, sweet and savoury at once: the perfume softens, and the caramel and walnut of Madeira come forward.

Brennan's carries both uses. Aged sherry finishes the Turtle Soup, with brown butter spinach and grated egg: a spoonful of nutty, dry sherry lifts the rich, dark soup the way lemon lifts fish. In some New Orleans dining rooms sherry also comes to the table in a small jug or cruet for the guest to add; whether Brennan's adds it in the kitchen, at the pass or at the table is a question for lineup.

On the dinner Creole Hanger Steak, broccolini is glazed with Madeira, the wine reduced until syrupy, a sweet, nutty counterweight to the Creole spice and chilli crisp. Neither bottle is named in the house notes, so never promise a producer, and tell every guest who avoids alcohol that the wine is there; never promise it has cooked off.

Truffle words on a menu promise different things. Fresh black truffle, Tuber melanosporum, from Périgord and elsewhere, is a winter tuber, in season roughly December to March; the summer truffle looks similar and tastes milder. Truffle essence and truffle juice come from cooked truffles. Much truffle oil, and some truffle butter and salt, is flavoured with a made aroma rather than truffle itself. Which of these is on a plate is a question for the kitchen, and the guest should hear the plain answer.

Say it simply: a rich brown sauce finished with Madeira, a fortified wine that tastes of caramel and walnut; with truffle, the black truffle of Périgord. For the turtle soup: finished with aged sherry from Jerez, nutty and dry, which cuts the richness.

ratios.label: Madère
ratios.value: About 7 parts reduced demi-glace to 1 part Madeira, the wine added off the heat

ratios.label: For 1 litre (about 1 quart) of demi-glace
ratios.value: About 150 ml (2/3 cup) of Madeira, port or sherry

ratios.label: Périgueux
ratios.value: Madère finished with truffle essence and chopped black truffle

faults.fault: Flat, sweetish sauce with no perfume
faults.cause: The wine went in too early or was boiled after it went in.
faults.fix: Add a fresh measure of wine off the heat just before service, and hold the sauce below a simmer.

faults.fault: Too thin once the wine is in
faults.cause: The demi-glace was not reduced enough to allow for the wine.
faults.fix: Reduce the base further before the wine goes in, or reduce a little more base and combine.

faults.cause: Too much wine for the sauce, or a raw, young wine.
faults.fix: Balance with more demi-glace and a piece of cold butter, then taste; next time measure the wine.

faults.cause: Truffle chopped hours ahead, or boiled hard in the sauce.
faults.fix: Chop it close to service, keep it in its essence and add it at the end.

cards.front: What is a fortified wine?
cards.back: Wine strengthened with grape spirit: Madeira, port and sherry are the three a sauce cook uses most.

cards.front: How is sauce madère made?
cards.back: Demi-glace reduced until thicker than needed, then Madeira added off the heat; strained and held hot without boiling.

cards.front: Why is the demi-glace reduced before the Madeira goes in?
cards.back: The wine thins the sauce, so the base is taken thicker first and the wine brings it back to coating thickness.

cards.front: Why is a fortified wine finish added late and never boiled hard?
cards.back: Heat drives off the perfume first, leaving a flat, sweetish sauce, and the perfume is what the wine is there for.

cards.front: What is sauce Périgueux?
cards.back: Madère with truffle essence and chopped black truffle, named for the capital of Périgord, the truffle country.

cards.front: How does périgourdine differ from Périgueux?
cards.back: The truffle is in slices or small balls rather than chopped, and some texts add foie gras.

cards.front: What is sauce financière?
cards.back: A Madeira sauce made richer with truffle, the sauce of an old garnish of chicken quenelles, mushrooms and truffle in a vol-au-vent.

cards.front: How is a Madeira glaze different from a Madeira finish?
cards.back: A glaze reduces the wine until syrupy, trading perfume for concentrated caramel and walnut; a finish adds it late to keep the perfume.

cards.front: What finishes the Brennan's Turtle Soup, and why?
cards.back: Aged sherry, with brown butter spinach and grated egg; its nutty, dry acidity lifts the rich soup the way lemon lifts fish.

cards.front: What does a server tell a guest who avoids alcohol about the turtle soup or the Madeira broccolini?
cards.back: That wine is in it, sherry in the soup and Madeira in the glaze, and never that the alcohol has cooked off.

cards.front: What can truffle oil on a menu honestly promise?
cards.back: Often only a truffle aroma: much truffle oil is flavoured with a made aroma, not truffle. Ask the kitchen which form is on the plate.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dish carries a Madeira glaze?
cards.back: The dinner Creole Hanger Steak, whose broccolini is glazed with Madeira, sweet and nutty against the Creole spice and chilli crisp.

questions.q: When does the Madeira go into a sauce madère?
questions.answer: Off the heat, once the base is reduced
distractors: At the start, with the mirepoix
Halfway through, boiled hard to cook it out
questions.why: The base is reduced first to allow for the wine; added off the heat and not boiled, the Madeira keeps its perfume.

questions.q: Why is a fortified wine finish never boiled hard?
distractors: It makes the sauce too thick
It thickens the sauce like a roux
It splits the demi-glace into fat
questions.why: The aroma is the first thing to go, leaving a flat, sweetish sauce; that is why the wine is added at the end.

questions.q: Sauce Périgueux is madère finished with what?
distractors: Diced beef marrow and chopped parsley
questions.why: Périgueux is named for the capital of Périgord, the black truffle country; périgourdine shows the truffle in slices or balls instead.

questions.q: What chiefly separates périgourdine from Périgueux?
questions.answer: Its truffle is sliced, not chopped
distractors: It uses port in place of the Madeira
It is thickened with egg yolks
It is made from fish stock
questions.why: Both are madère with truffle; périgourdine shows the truffle in slices or small balls, and some texts add foie gras.

questions.q: What does a Madeira glaze, such as the one on the Creole Hanger Steak's broccolini, do with the wine?
distractors: Adds it raw at the table
Sets it alight at the pass
questions.why: A glaze is the exception to the late-finish rule: reduced with butter or stock, the wine turns sweet and savoury and clings.

questions.q: Which fortified wine finishes the Brennan's Turtle Soup?
questions.why: The house finishes the soup with aged sherry, along with brown butter spinach and grated egg; its nutty dryness cuts the richness.

questions.q: A guest who avoids alcohol orders the turtle soup. What does the server say?
questions.answer: That the soup is finished with sherry
distractors: Nothing, because the alcohol cooks off
That it holds only a trace of vinegar
That cooking wine carries no alcohol
questions.why: The house notes say to tell guests who avoid alcohol that the sherry is there; saying it has cooked off would be a promise nobody can check.

questions.q: What makes a wine such as Madeira fortified?
questions.why: Madeira, port and sherry are strengthened with grape spirit, which raises their alcohol and shapes their sweetness and keeping.

questions.q: A menu says truffle oil. What can a server honestly promise?
questions.answer: Only a truffle aroma; ask the kitchen
distractors: Fresh Périgord truffle shaved at the table
Whole truffle infused for a year
questions.why: Much truffle oil is flavoured with a made aroma rather than truffle, so the server promises only what the kitchen confirms.

entries.title: The hollandaise and béarnaise families
entries.summary: The daughters of hollandaise and béarnaise: mousseline, maltaise, Mikado, noisette and moutarde on one side, Paloise, Choron and Foyot on the other. Each is acid, yolks and butter with one defining addition.
entries.guest: These are warm butter sauces thickened with egg yolk, each with one extra note: whipped cream, blood orange, brown butter, mustard, mint, tomato or a reduced meat glaze.

paras: Hollandaise and béarnaise are the two warm emulsions of the classical kitchen: egg yolks holding warm butter in fine droplets, sharpened with acid. Hollandaise takes lemon or a plain vinegar reduction; béarnaise is built on a reduction of white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot and herbs. From each comes a family, and the rule that governs it is short: an acid, yolks, butter, then one defining addition. Know the addition and you know the sauce.

Because the base is the same, so are the dangers. Every daughter scrambles if it overheats and splits if the butter goes in too fast, and each addition brings a risk of its own: water from juice, weight from cream, heat from brown butter.

Make the mother first, then add. Whisk the yolks with the reduction over barely simmering water to a thick ribbon, about 65°C (149°F), mount the warm butter off the heat and season. Only then does the defining addition go in, and how it goes in matters.

Folded additions go in last and gently: whipped cream for mousseline, just before the plate leaves. Liquid additions are reduced first, so they flavour without thinning: blood orange or mandarin juice cooked down by half, then whisked in with fine zest. Butter additions replace the plain butter: for noisette, cook the butter until the milk solids brown and it smells of hazelnut, then let it cool to warm, about 60°C (140°F), before it meets the yolks. Herb additions are split between the reduction and the finish: mint stalks in the vinegar for Paloise, chopped mint at the end.

Mousseline, also called Chantilly, is hollandaise with lightly whipped cream folded in, about one part cream to three or four of sauce: lighter, paler and softer, for poached fish and asparagus. Maltaise is hollandaise with blood orange juice and grated zest, named for the blood oranges of Malta, and the classic sauce for asparagus. Mikado does the same with mandarin. Noisette is hollandaise made with brown butter, beurre noisette, darker and nutty in taste; the name describes the butter's colour. Moutarde is hollandaise finished with Dijon mustard, sharp enough for grilled fish.

Paloise, named for Pau, the old capital of Béarn, is béarnaise with mint in place of tarragon, in the reduction and the finish, for lamb. Choron is béarnaise with tomato cooked down to a thick paste. Foyot is béarnaise with glace de viande, reduced meat glaze, whisked in, tawny and deep, and many texts call the same sauce Valois; both have an entry of their own. Further out sit rare names such as Arlésienne and Tyrolienne, which the old books record and describe differently; they show how far the family runs.

Too much juice in a maltaise or Mikado thins the sauce and can split it, so reduce the juice first. Cream folded in too early collapses in the heat and leaves a mousseline loose and greasy; fold it in at the pass. Brown butter added hot scrambles the yolks, and butter taken too dark turns a noisette bitter; cool it to warm and stop at hazelnut brown. Mint chopped long before service blackens and loses its scent. For a split or scrambled base, the rescue is the hollandaise rescue, taught with breaking and rescuing.

The house's own notes read the menu as a lesson in this family: plain hollandaise on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, Choron on the Eggs Sardou and Foyot on the Roasted Chateaubriand. A server who knows the family can describe all four sauces from one idea.

Describe the base, then the addition: a warm butter sauce thickened with egg yolk, with blood orange, or lightened with whipped cream, or with mint for lamb. The name noisette comes from the colour of browned butter; whether a sauce carries nuts, egg or anything else a guest asks about is a question for the kitchen.

ratios.label: Mousseline
ratios.value: About 1 part lightly whipped cream to 3 or 4 parts hollandaise, folded in at the last moment

ratios.label: Maltaise, for a hollandaise of 3 yolks
ratios.value: The juice of 1 blood orange, reduced by half, with a little grated zest

ratios.label: Noisette
ratios.value: Brown butter in place of the plain butter, cooled to warm before it goes in

ratios.label: Paloise
ratios.value: Mint in place of tarragon: stalks in the reduction, chopped leaves to finish

temps.label: The yolks thicken into a ribbon
Brown butter cooled to warm before it meets the yolks

faults.cause: Too much juice, or juice added without reducing it.
faults.fix: Reduce the juice by half before it goes in; whisk a thin sauce, drop by drop, into a fresh yolk warmed over the bain-marie.

faults.cause: Whipped cream folded in too early, or into sauce that was too hot.
faults.fix: Fold the cream in just before service, into sauce that is warm, never hot.

faults.cause: Brown butter added hot, or taken past hazelnut brown.
faults.fix: Stop the browning at hazelnut, pour the butter into a cold bowl and let it cool to warm before mounting.

faults.fault: Black, dull mint in a Paloise
faults.cause: Mint chopped long before service, or cooked hard.
faults.fix: Chop the mint at the last moment and stir it in off the heat.

cards.front: What is the rule of the hollandaise and béarnaise families?
cards.back: An acid, egg yolks, butter, then one defining addition: know the addition and you know the sauce.

cards.front: What is sauce mousseline, and what else is it called?
cards.back: Hollandaise with lightly whipped cream folded in, lighter and paler, for fish and asparagus; it is also called sauce Chantilly.

cards.front: What is sauce maltaise, and what is its classic partner?
cards.back: Hollandaise with blood orange juice and grated zest, named for the blood oranges of Malta; the classic sauce for asparagus.

cards.front: What is sauce Mikado?
cards.back: Hollandaise flavoured with mandarin juice and zest: the maltaise idea with a different citrus.

cards.front: What is sauce noisette?
cards.back: Hollandaise made with brown butter, beurre noisette; the name means hazelnut, for the colour and smell of the browned butter.

cards.front: What is sauce moutarde in the hollandaise family?
cards.back: Hollandaise finished with Dijon mustard, a sharper sauce for grilled fish.

cards.front: What is sauce Paloise, and what is it served with?
cards.back: Béarnaise with mint in place of tarragon, in the reduction and the finish; named for Pau, in Béarn, and served with lamb.

cards.front: Which two béarnaise daughters are on the Brennan's menu, and what does each add?
cards.back: Choron adds tomato cooked down to a paste, on the Eggs Sardou; Foyot adds glace de viande, on the Roasted Chateaubriand.

cards.front: What is sauce Valois?
cards.back: In many texts, a second name for Foyot: béarnaise with glace de viande. Some authors draw a line between the two.

cards.front: Why is the juice reduced before it goes into a maltaise?
cards.back: Raw juice adds water that thins the emulsion and can split it; reduced by half, it flavours without loosening.

cards.front: Why must brown butter cool before it goes into a noisette?
cards.back: Straight from the pan it is far hotter than the yolks can bear and scrambles them; cooled to about 60°C (140°F), it mounts smoothly.

cards.front: When is the whipped cream folded into a mousseline?
cards.back: At the last moment, into warm sauce; folded in early, it collapses and leaves the sauce loose.

questions.q: What do all the daughters of hollandaise and béarnaise share?
questions.answer: Acid, yolks, butter and one addition
distractors: A roux of flour cooked in clarified butter
Milk infused with onion and clove
questions.why: Every member is a warm yolk and butter emulsion sharpened with acid; one defining addition gives each its name.

questions.q: Which sauce is hollandaise with whipped cream folded in?
questions.why: Mousseline, also called Chantilly, is lightened with whipped cream; maltaise adds blood orange, Paloise mint and noisette brown butter.

questions.q: Which sauce, made with blood orange, is the classic partner of asparagus?
questions.why: Maltaise is hollandaise with blood orange juice and zest, named for the blood oranges of Malta, and the classic sauce for asparagus.

questions.q: Sauce Paloise replaces the tarragon of béarnaise with what?
questions.why: Paloise, named for Pau in Béarn, uses mint in the reduction and the finish, which suits lamb.

questions.q: What gives sauce noisette its name?
questions.why: Noisette means hazelnut: the sauce is made with butter browned to that colour and smell. Any question about nuts goes to the kitchen.

questions.q: When does the whipped cream go into a mousseline?
questions.answer: At the last moment, into warm sauce
distractors: With the yolks, before the butter
Into the butter before it is mounted
Once the sauce has been chilled
questions.why: Folded in early or into hot sauce, the cream collapses and leaves the mousseline loose and greasy, so it goes in at the pass.

questions.q: A maltaise has come out thin. What is the usual cause?
questions.answer: Raw juice added without reducing it
distractors: Too little lemon in the base
Butter that had been clarified first
questions.why: Juice is mostly water; reduced by half first, it flavours the sauce without loosening the emulsion or risking a split.

questions.q: Before brown butter goes into a noisette, it should cool to about what?
questions.why: Hot brown butter scrambles the yolks; warm butter, about the heat of the finished sauce, mounts smoothly.

questions.q: Which two sauces on the Brennan's menu are daughters of béarnaise?
questions.why: Choron, béarnaise with tomato, is on the Eggs Sardou, and Foyot, béarnaise with meat glaze, on the Roasted Chateaubriand; maltaise and mousseline come from hollandaise, and marchand de vin is brown.
